We begin with the universal decomposition of any observable $Y$ conditioned on state $X$ into a deterministic trend $\mu(X)$ and an orthogonal residual $\epsilon(X)$. This establishes the theoretical target for all predictive engines. However, the realization of this target is severely constrained by the small-sample bias-variance tradeoff. When the signal-to-noise ratio is low ($\sigma \gg$ signal amplitude) and $n$ is small, the variance introduced by estimating the parameters of the true functional form exceeds the inherent bias of simply predicting the constant mean. Consequently, sophisticated models collapse to trivial baselines. To navigate this, the ExCal anomaly detection primitive bypasses explicit parametric fitting entirely. Instead, it operates on the geometry of the residuals themselves—specifically, the subspace residuals $[\mathbf{z}_t, \Delta\mathbf{z}_t]$ derived via PCA. By calibrating these residuals against robust percentile floors and applying prevalence damping, ExCal identifies structural breaks without suffering from the catastrophic variance inflation that plagues standard regression in sparse regimes. Thus, the three primitives form a closed logical loop: decomposition defines the truth, bias-variance analysis dictates when truth cannot be learned, and excess calibration provides a non-parametric fallback to detect deviations from the learnable manifold.
